opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, because human intuition is really unreliable when you're staring at your own model's outputs every day. When you're working on a generative model, especially for 3D, it's very easy to fall in love with a handful of cherry-picked examples. You change something, generate a few assets, and think, "Wow, this looks much better." But you might just be looking at the prompts where the new version happens to shine, or you're biased because you want the change you spent two weeks on to work.

3D makes this even harder than images. A model can look great from the front view in a thumbnail, but when you rotate it, the back is broken, the topology is messy, the texture has seams, or the geometry doesn't hold up when an artist actually imports it into Blender or a game engine. So "it looks better" is not a well-defined statement unless you specify better on what, for whom, and across what distribution of inputs.

So for us, systematic evaluation means a few things. First, a fixed, representative benchmark set of prompts and images that reflects what users actually ask for, not what we wish they'd ask for. Second, blind comparisons, where the people judging don't know which output came from which model, so you remove that emotional attachment. Third, looking at many dimensions separately: geometry quality, texture quality, prompt alignment, consistency across views, usability downstream. A change might improve texture and quietly hurt geometry, and if you only have one vague overall impression, you'll miss that trade-off.

The other reason is speed of iteration. As a startup, we have limited compute and limited people. If every decision is a debate based on gut feelings, the team gets stuck, or worse, the loudest opinion wins. If you have a trusted evaluation pipeline, you can run an experiment, get a number, and make a decision in a day. That compounds. Over a year, the team that iterates with reliable feedback just moves much faster than the team that relies on vibes.

And finally, it's about respecting users. People pay us and build real things on top of our models. Shipping a regression because a few demos looked nice is a real cost to them. Objective evaluation is how you make sure each release is actually a step forward, not just a step sideways that looks good in a tweet.

r001.rationale: It says developers may favor a change because they want the work they spent time on to succeed, leading them to overvalue selected outputs.

r002.rationale: It proposes blind comparisons where judges do not know which model produced each output, which communicates comparing outputs from the old and new versions without revealing their source.

r003.rationale: It does not say that blinded comparisons often show the old version outperforming the new one.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The short answer is that with generative 3D, your eyes will lie to you. Not because anyone is being dishonest, but because the output is so visually rich that it's incredibly easy to fool yourself.

Here's what happens in practice. Someone on the team trains a new checkpoint, they generate a handful of models, maybe a sword, a chair, a cartoon character, and they look great. Everyone gets excited. But those three or five examples are a tiny sample from an enormous distribution of prompts and images that users actually send us. And people naturally gravitate toward the prompts that look good. So you end up with a kind of selection bias built into the demo. You ship it, and then a week later users tell you that hands got worse, or the topology is messier on organic shapes, or texture seams are showing up where they didn't before. The new model was better on the things you looked at and worse on the things you didn't.

The other issue is that 3D quality is multi-dimensional in a way that's really hard to hold in your head. There's geometry accuracy, there's mesh quality and topology, there's texture fidelity, there's how well the result matches the prompt or the reference image, there's how usable the asset is downstream in a game engine. A change that improves one of those often quietly degrades another. If you're just eyeballing results, you'll notice the improvement because that's what you were looking for, and you'll miss the regression.

So for us, having a fixed evaluation set with a wide spread of categories, running the same prompts through old and new models, and scoring them both with automated metrics and with blind human preference comparisons, that's not bureaucracy. It's the only way to know whether we actually made progress or whether we just got lucky on a few samples. We've definitely had cases where a change we were sure was a win turned out to be neutral or slightly negative once we measured it properly. That's humbling, but it's far better to learn that internally than from users.

And there's a compounding effect. Model development is a long sequence of small decisions. If each decision is made on vibes, the errors accumulate and you can drift in a direction nobody intended. If each one is grounded in measurement, even imperfect measurement, those small wins stack up reliably. That's really what lets a team iterate fast without constantly second-guessing whether they're moving forward.

r001.rationale: The response describes selection bias and how developers can miss regressions, but it does not identify self-protective bias as a reason they overestimate their own models.

r002.rationale: It proposes running the same prompts through old and new models and using blind human preference comparisons, which communicates comparing versions without revealing their identity.

r003.rationale: It says some presumed improvements proved neutral or slightly negative, but does not say blinded comparisons often find the old version performs better.

astra-6.text: Because with generative models, it’s very easy to convince yourself that a new version is better by picking a few impressive examples. But that doesn’t tell you whether it’s consistently better for users. You need to compare models across a broad set of prompts, under the same conditions, and evaluate different aspects of the result—does it follow the prompt, does the geometry make sense, and how good are the textures? Otherwise, you might improve one aspect while making another worse and not notice. A systematic evaluation gives us a reliable feedback loop, so we can distinguish real progress from cherry-picking or personal preference.

sol-6.1.text:
With generative models, it’s very easy to look at a few impressive examples and feel that the model has improved. But those examples might be cherry-picked, or the new model might be better at one category and worse at another. So we need a systematic way to compare versions across a broad range of inputs and understand whether the improvement is consistent.

For 3D, that also means looking beyond whether a rendered image looks good. We need to consider the geometry, the textures, how well the result follows the prompt, and whether the asset is useful to the user. Having consistent evaluation gives us a more reliable signal for deciding which changes actually move the product forward.

r001.rationale: The response mentions cherry-picked examples and uneven performance, but does not identify developers’ self-protective bias as a reason they overestimate their models.

r002.rationale: It proposes comparing model versions across inputs, but does not say to hide which version produced each output.

r003.rationale: It does not report that blinded comparisons often show the old Meshy version performing better.
